title: Little scientists
intro: Scientists observe, wonder and check. You can too!

lessons.title: Looking like a scientist
lessons.intro: A scientist looks calmly and notices what others miss. Today we'll learn to observe with a magnifying glass and a notebook.
lessons.closing: Observing means looking calmly, writing and drawing, without touching. With that, you're already becoming a scientist!

exercises.prompt: Listen. A scientist also observes with their ears. Who's making that sound?
options: A cricket
A bee
A frog
exercises.explanation: It's a cricket: the male sings by rubbing one wing against the other. Listening carefully is observing too.

exercises.prompt: Is this how a scientist observes? Put each one in its box.
bins: This is how a scientist observes

sortItems.label: Looking calmly and quietly
Writing and drawing what they see
Using the magnifying glass in the shade
Grabbing the insect to see it better
Making noise so it moves
Holding the magnifying glass in the sun over the insect

exercises.explanation: If you grab it or scare it, the insect stops what it was doing and you can't see how it really lives. And a magnifying glass in the sun focuses the light and can burn it.

exercises.prompt: What is a magnifying glass for?
options: To make small things look bigger
To catch insects
To light things up at night
exercises.explanation: Its lens enlarges what you look at: that's how you discover legs, tiny hairs and eyes you can barely see with your eyes alone.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: In my field notebook I write the ___, the ___ and what the insect is doing, and I ___ it.
exercises.explanation: With the date and place you can compare with another day or another spot, and drawing makes you notice every detail.

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: each tool with what it helps you do.
exercises.explanation: They're simple tools that help you observe better without bothering anyone: the ruler, for example, goes next to the insect, never on top of it.

lessons.title: Asking and guessing
lessons.intro: Paquito wonders about lots of things. So do scientists: they ask a question, think about what will happen and check it.
lessons.closing: Observe, ask, make a hypothesis, check and conclude: that's the scientific method. And being wrong teaches you too!

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of the scientific method in order.
exercises.explanation: First you look, which gives you a question; then you think about what will happen, you check it, and at the end you work out what you learned.

exercises.prompt: Can it be checked? Put each question in its box.
bins: Can be checked by looking or counting

sortItems.label: Which flower do bees visit most?
Are there more pill bugs in the sun or in the shade?
At what time do crickets sing most?
Which insect is the prettiest?
What do ants think of me?

exercises.explanation: Flower visits, pill bugs and songs can be counted. What's pretty depends on each person's taste, and what an ant thinks can't be seen or counted.

exercises.prompt: What is a hypothesis?
options: What I think will happen, and why
The sure answer
A very rare insect
exercises.explanation: It's an idea to put to the test: you don't know yet if it's true, and that's why you do the experiment.

exercises.prompt: Your hypothesis was wrong. What does a good scientist do?
options: Writes down what happened and learns from it
Erases the results
Gives up
exercises.explanation: A hypothesis that turns out wrong still teaches you something: now you know something new, and you get another question to keep exploring.

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: each step with its example.

pairs.right: “I think the sunflower, because it's yellow”
“We counted 7 bees on the sunflower and 2 on the other one”
“This time, the bees preferred the sunflower”

exercises.explanation: Each step answers something different: what I want to know, what I think, what I saw and what I learned.

lessons.title: Experiments that do no harm
lessons.intro: Which flower do bees prefer? Where are there more pill bugs? Let's find out with experiments that don't hurt anyone.
lessons.closing: A good experiment is fair and respectful: you change only one thing, and the insects stay free and at home.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you can do in an experiment with insects.

items.label: Look at them with a magnifying glass, in the shade
Count them and write it down
Compare the visits to two flowers
Lift a leaf gently and put it back as it was
Put pill bugs in a closed jar

exercises.explanation: In a closed jar a pill bug gets scared and dries out, and you no longer see how it really lives. Everything else is done without touching it and leaving things in place.

exercises.prompt: You want to find out which flower bees prefer. Which experiment is fair?
options: Count for 5 minutes at each flower, at the same time of day
Watch one flower for 1 minute and the other for 1 hour
Catch the bees and release them onto one flower
exercises.explanation: If you watch one flower longer, it will get more visits even if it isn't the favorite. With the same time and the same hour, only the flower changes, so the comparison is fair.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Pill bugs need ___ to breathe, so they are usually in the ___.
exercises.explanation: They're cousins of shrimp and breathe through body parts that must stay damp. In the sun they'd dry out, so they look for shade under leaves and stones.

exercises.prompt: Which flower color is hardest for a bee to see?
options: Red
Blue
Yellow
exercises.explanation: A bee's eyes pick up blue, purple and yellow very well, but red looks dark to them. That's why many of the flowers they visit are blue, purple or yellow.

exercises.prompt: Put the pill bug experiment in order.

steps.label: Make the hypothesis: “There will be more in the shade”
With an adult, gently lift leaves in the sun and in the shade
Count the pill bugs and write it down
Put everything back as it was

exercises.explanation: First you think, then you check and write it down. And always, at the end, everything goes back in place so the pill bugs stay in their home.

lessons.title: A hotel for insects
lessons.intro: With canes, pine cones and wood you can build a shelter for solitary bees and ladybugs. Who will come to stay?
lessons.closing: An insect hotel, near flowers and without poison, is a gift for the bugs in your neighborhood. And it lets you watch them up close!

exercises.prompt: Where will a solitary bee hide? Tap the spot.
exercises.explanation: Solitary bees look for narrow tunnels, like the canes, to leave their eggs with pollen and seal the entrance.

exercises.prompt: Is it good for the hotel? Put each one in its box.

sortItems.label: Hollow canes
Pine cones
Wood with holes
Twigs and bark
Plastic bags
Closed bottles

exercises.explanation: Insects look for natural materials with holes and gaps that let air through. Plastic doesn't breathe, it traps damp and whatever is inside goes moldy.

exercises.prompt: Tap the ones that can stay at the hotel.
exercises.explanation: The solitary bee nests in the canes and the ladybug shelters among pine cones and bark. Mosquitoes and dragonflies don't use it: their young grow up in water.

exercises.prompt: Where is the best place for the hotel?
options: Where it gets the morning sun, out of the rain and near flowers
Inside a dark closet
On the ground, where puddles form
exercises.explanation: Bees need the sun's warmth to start flying in the morning, a dry hotel doesn't rot, and nearby flowers give them food.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Solitary bees almost never sting because they have no ___ to defend. Each mother seals her nest with ___.
exercises.explanation: Hive bees defend their whole family; a solitary bee lives alone and has no reason to attack. The mud protects her eggs while they grow.

lessons.title: The planet and insects
lessons.intro: Insects need a planet with plants, clean water and dark nights. And there are lots of small things we can do for them.
lessons.closing: A flower planted, a light turned off, a wild corner: every small action counts. Insects notice!

exercises.prompt: Put each action in its box.

sortItems.label: Planting flowers
Turning off lights that aren't being used at night
Leaving a corner with wild plants
Spraying poison all over the garden
Leaving trash in the park
Cutting down every plant in the yard

exercises.explanation: Flowers and wild plants give them food and shelter, and dark nights let them find each other. Poison, trash and removing every plant take away their home and food.

exercises.prompt: Why does turning off unused lights at night help?
options: Fireflies look for each other with their light, and moths get confused by lamps
Because that makes all insects go away
Because insects are afraid of the dark
exercises.explanation: With fewer lamps on, fireflies can see their partner's light and moths go on their way instead of circling a light bulb.

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: each problem with something we can do.

pairs.right: Turn off the ones not in use

exercises.explanation: For every problem there's something small we can do. Ladybugs, for example, control aphids without poison and without harming bees.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: A pot of ___ on the windowsill gives food to ___.
exercises.explanation: Even a small pot of flowers offers nectar and pollen to bees and other pollinators passing through the city.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you can do this week to help insects.

items.label: Turn off lights I'm not using
Leave dry leaves in a corner of the yard
Cut all the flowers in the yard

exercises.explanation: Planting, turning off lights and leaving dry leaves (where beetles and pill bugs shelter) are small actions you can do yourself. Catching or cutting everything takes away their freedom and food.

lessons.title: Expert forest ranger
lessons.intro: You've learned so much about insects. Now it's time to make the expert forest ranger's promise.
lessons.closing: Observe, respect, care and teach: that's your promise. Insects have a great friend in you!

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: each part of the promise with what it means.

pairs.right: Look calmly and write in the notebook
Leave each insect in its home
Plant flowers and not use poison
Help others not to be afraid

exercises.explanation: All four go together: when you observe you learn, when you learn you respect, and what you know you can care for and teach.

exercises.prompt: Your cousin screams when he sees a butterfly. What do you do as an expert forest ranger?
options: I calmly explain it's harmless and we watch it together from a distance
I make fun of him
I chase the butterfly away with a newspaper
exercises.explanation: Fear goes away as you get to know something: if you tell him what you know and you watch it calmly together, he may start to like it.

exercises.prompt: Put in order how to take an insect out of the house without hurting it.

steps.label: Gently place a cup over it
Slide a piece of cardboard underneath
Let it go near some plants

exercises.explanation: The cup covers it without touching it and the cardboard acts as a door; that way it travels safely to the plants, where it can go on with its life.

exercises.prompt: Does an expert forest ranger do it? Put each one in its box.

sortItems.label: Watch calmly from a distance
Tell a friend what they learned
Plant flowers
Tell an adult if they see one that stings
Keep insects in a jar
Spray poison all over the yard

exercises.explanation: A forest ranger takes care of insects and of themselves too: that's why they watch from a distance and tell an adult. Shutting them in or poisoning them causes harm.

exercises.prompt: Complete your promise.
exercises.sentence: An expert forest ranger observes, ___, cares and ___ others not to be afraid.
exercises.explanation: These are the four promises of an expert forest ranger. With them you take care of insects and help others love them too.

exam.title: Unit challenge
exam.intro: Hexa's very last challenge! Show everything a little scientist does. If you pass it, you'll be an expert forest ranger.
exam.closing: You did it! You observe, ask, check and take care of insects. Now it's your turn to teach others to love them.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of the scientific method in order.
exercises.explanation: Each step comes from the one before: what you observe gives you a question, the hypothesis gets checked and the result leads you to the conclusion.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Who's making that sound?
options: A bee
A cricket
A frog
exercises.explanation: It's a bee's buzz: it beats its wings about 200 times a second, and that super-fast flapping is what we hear.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: What I think will happen is called a ___, and what I learn at the end is called a ___.
exercises.explanation: The hypothesis comes before checking, when you don't know yet; the conclusion comes after, once you've looked and counted.

exercises.prompt: Tap what helps insects.

items.label: Turn off unused lights at night

exercises.explanation: Flowers, shelters and dark nights give them food, a home and a way to find each other. Catching them or cutting all the flowers takes exactly that away.

exercises.prompt: You want to find out what time crickets sing most. What is the fairest way?
options: Listen for the same amount of time at each hour and write it down
Listen only when you remember
Catch a cricket and listen to it at home
exercises.explanation: If you listen for the same time every time, only the hour changes and you can compare. And the crickets stay free, singing where they live.

exercises.prompt: Put each action in its box.

sortItems.label: Picking up trash in the park
Leaving dry leaves in a corner
Letting ladybugs eat the aphids
Spraying the whole garden
Leaving lights on all night

exercises.explanation: Clean places, wild corners and natural helpers keep insects safe. Poison everywhere and lights all night harm or confuse them.

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: each tool with its use.

pairs.right: Take an insect out of the house without harming it

exercises.explanation: They all help you get to know and care for insects without harming them: looking, writing, measuring from a distance and returning them to their place.

exercises.prompt: Where would you put the insect hotel?
options: In the morning sun, out of the rain and near flowers
In a dark, wet corner
Next to a lamp that's on all night
exercises.explanation: The morning sun warms the bees so they can head out to fly, a dry spot keeps the hotel from rotting, and the flowers give them food nearby.

exercises.prompt: Does an expert forest ranger do it? Put each one in its box.

sortItems.label: Observe calmly and take notes
Help a friend not to be afraid
Let insects go free
Squash a bug for no reason
Hold a magnifying glass in the sun over an insect

exercises.explanation: Observing, teaching and letting go is caring. Squashing for no reason or burning with a magnifying glass harms a living thing that has its role in nature.

exercises.prompt: Tap the ones that can stay at an insect hotel.
exercises.explanation: Solitary bees nest in the canes and ladybugs shelter among pine cones and bark. Dragonflies and mosquitoes grow up in water, so they look for puddles and ponds.
